nodes.title: Google Kubernetes Engine: Key Ideas
nodes.content: GKE is GCP's managed Kubernetes service — two flavors: Standard (you manage node pools) and Autopilot (Google manages nodes, you only pay for pod resources). Exam questions test node pools, networking, identity, and which mode to pick.

flashcards.front: GKE Standard vs Autopilot — which to pick?
flashcards.back: Standard: you create and size node pools, pay for nodes whether pods use them or not, full control. Autopilot: Google sizes nodes automatically, you pay only for pods' CPU/RAM/storage, hands-off but less flexibility (e.g., DaemonSets restricted). Pick Autopilot for new projects; Standard when you need GPUs, large nodes, or custom OS.

A group of nodes with the same machine type, OS, and config inside a GKE cluster. You can have multiple pools (e.g., default + gpu-pool + high-memory-pool). Pods can be scheduled to specific pools via node selectors or taints. Upgrades happen per pool, so prod and batch can be on different K8s versions.

Lets a Kubernetes Service Account impersonate a Google Cloud Service Account — pods get GCP IAM permissions without long-lived JSON keys. Replaces the dangerous pattern of mounting `gcp-sa-key.json` as a secret. Always-on by default in Autopilot; opt-in for Standard.

VPC-native: pods get IPs from a secondary range of your VPC — direct routing, no overlay overhead, supports private GKE. Routes-based: legacy, uses GCP routes table (limited to 200 routes per VPC). All new clusters should be VPC-native; routes-based is for legacy compatibility only.

nodes.title: Networking fundamentals: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Networking moves packets between machines using layered protocols (the OSI / TCP-IP stack). Most exam questions test routing decisions, subnetting math, the difference between L2 and L3, and how DNS / DHCP make the whole thing usable for humans.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between Layer 2 and Layer 3?
flashcards.back: L2 (data link) uses MAC addresses to deliver frames inside a single broadcast domain (a switch). L3 (network) uses IP addresses to route packets between networks (a router). Switches do L2; routers do L3.

flashcards.front: How does a subnet mask work?
flashcards.back: The mask splits an IP into a network portion (the high bits, set to 1) and a host portion (the low bits, set to 0). `/24` means the first 24 bits are network = up to 256 hosts (254 usable). `/30` is 4 IPs = 2 hosts — typical for a point-to-point link.

Domain Name System translates human-readable names (`example.com`) into IP addresses. A recursive resolver asks the root, the TLD server (`.com`), and finally the authoritative server for the domain. TTL controls how long answers are cached.

flashcards.front: TCP vs UDP — when do you pick each?
flashcards.back: TCP is reliable, ordered, congestion-controlled — use it when every byte matters (HTTP, SSH, SMTP). UDP is lightweight, no handshake, no retransmit — use it for streaming, gaming, DNS queries, anywhere latency beats reliability.

nodes.title: Identity and access management: Key Ideas
nodes.content: IAM is the layer that decides who can do what. It's almost always the first thing to misconfigure and the most common security failure mode. Every cloud uses the same primitives — identities, policies, roles — under slightly different names.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between authentication and authorization?
flashcards.back: Authentication (AuthN) proves who you are — password, MFA, certificate. Authorization (AuthZ) decides what you're allowed to do once authenticated — policies, roles, ACLs. AuthN happens first; AuthZ is checked on every request.

flashcards.front: What is a role (vs a user)?
flashcards.back: A user is a long-lived identity tied to a person. A role is a short-lived, assumable identity — services or users 'become' the role to get temporary credentials. Roles let you grant access without sharing long-term keys. Always prefer roles.

Identity-based policies attach to a user / role and say what THEY can do. Resource-based policies attach to a thing (S3 bucket, KMS key, SQS queue) and say who can access IT. Cross-account access usually needs both: target's resource policy says 'allow this account', source identity policy says 'allow this action on that resource'.

Instead of creating cloud users for every employee, federate from your corporate identity provider (Okta, Azure AD, Google Workspace). Users sign in once with their work account; the IdP issues a SAML / OIDC token; the cloud trades it for temporary credentials. One source of truth, instant deprovisioning.
